before: • For future entrants, require completed carpentry apprenticeship and Certificate III evidence. For existing workers, recognise reliably verified equivalent competence and address identified gaps. Select assessment methods proportionately to authorised scope and applicant risk.
after: • For future entrants, use completed carpentry apprenticeship and Certificate III evidence to establish baseline technical competence. For existing workers, recognise reliably verified equivalent competence and address identified gaps. Avoid duplicate whole-of-trade testing where reliable outcomes are already demonstrated; justify any additional licensing assessment by its specific purpose.

before: Risk should be assessed by consequence of failure, likelihood of non-compliance, whether mandatory standards apply, the difficulty of detecting defects before concealment, and the degree of independent judgment exercised. Contract value should not be used as the sole or decisive proxy for work risk.
after: Risk should be assessed by consequence of failure, mandatory standards, concealed conditions and the independent judgment exercised. Ordinary repairs should remain practicable within a carpenter’s demonstrated competence and lawful authority. Discovering rot does not automatically require specialist referral. The reason for additional input should be specific, such as work outside lawful scope, an unresolved safety or design issue, or a required specialist approval. Contract value can affect contracting requirements but should not alone define technical competence or permit obligations.

before: Match each requirement to the risk it controls and the burden it imposes. Current regulation 6 fixes the major domestic building contract threshold at $10,000; section 3 defines a major contract by an amount above that threshold, and section 29 requires registration authorising the work. Separate draft contract regulations propose $20,000. The departmental reply reports expected commencement on 31 March 2027; that is not a carpenter-scheme commencement date or proof that the threshold has changed. Low-value work can still create serious technical risk. [9–12]
after: Keep administration proportionate for routine, low-value jobs. Do not impose major domestic building contract documentation solely because a carpenter is registered where applicable law does not require it; retain other applicable consumer, permit and insurance obligations. Regulation 6 fixes the major-contract threshold at $10,000; sections 3 and 29 address the threshold and appropriately authorised registration. Separate draft contract regulations propose $20,000. The departmental reply reports expected commencement on 31 March 2027; that is not carpenter-scheme commencement or proof the threshold has changed. Reassess scope and contracting arrangements when discoveries expand a job. No new carpenter contract-value cap is proposed here. [9–12]

Proposed scope should be tested across residential outdoor carpentry as well as work inside homes: decks, verandahs, fences, gates and appropriate shed carpentry. These examples require work-specific mapping; they are not blanket permissions for whole structures, retaining walls or other regulated activities. Select replacement timber using the applicable dimensions, strength grade, durability or treatment, spans, loads and connections. An imperial description or larger member alone does not establish equivalent performance. Building-permit requirements and barrier requirements are separate: a deck below one metre is not automatically permit-exempt. Follow applicable planning approvals, building permits, approved design and specialist responsibilities. [13–14]

before: • Existing-building uncertainty, progressive discovery and the need to stop, investigate or refer.
after: • Existing-building uncertainty and progressive discovery: make unsafe areas safe, explain changed conditions to the owner, reassess the affected scope and pause affected work where safety, authority or required approvals remain unresolved. Continue work within established competence and lawful scope; obtain other practitioner input when a specific boundary requires it.

before: Employees and subcontractors performing the same prescribed residential carpentry work should meet the same technical competence standard. Apply separate role requirements where responsibilities and authority differ. Employees should not face business or financial requirements unrelated to their work authority. Subcontractor requirements should address relevant business, contractual, probity and insurance responsibilities only where justified. Confirm statutory terminology, legislative feasibility and insurance consequences before finalising the mechanism. [6, slide 3]
after: Employees and subcontractors performing the same prescribed residential carpentry work should meet the same technical competence standard. For employees working under a builder, completed apprenticeship and Certificate III evidence should normally establish the baseline technical outcome, subject to any lawful registration conditions. Independent business operation calls for additional relevant business and contracting requirements; it does not automatically establish advanced technical capability or authority to contract for every project. Requirements should follow responsibilities, authority and risk, rather than imposing unrelated business or financial obligations on employees. [6, slide 3]

before: Authority and handoff boundaries. Registration to perform prescribed carpentry work should not, by implication, authorise consumer contracting, building-permit responsibility, project-level supervision or coordination, structural design or certification, or specialist regulated work. The final framework should state when a carpenter must stop, refer or work under the authority of a registered builder, engineer, building surveyor or licensed specialist practitioner.
after: Authority and handoff boundaries. Distinguish baseline permission to perform prescribed work, requirements for independent business operation, and any additional assessed authority for defined residential work. Technical registration does not itself confer unrestricted consumer contracting, project supervision, structural design or certification, or specialist-trade authority. Consider a bounded progression route for experienced carpenters where evidence supports it, while retaining builders’, engineers’, building surveyors’ and licensed trades’ responsibilities. Extra labour or a larger budget does not resolve an authority or design boundary.

Optional modules could be tested for defined existing-building renovation, outdoor structures, or other specified work, including retaining-wall tasks only where competence, design and approval boundaries are established. Assess the function, consumer benefit, business obligations and insurance before granting additional authority. RRC, an endorsement or a revised existing class remain possible mechanisms; none is predetermined. Any future financial limit needs separate justification. No new monetary cap is selected or proposed in this submission.

before: For future entrants, this initiative recommends a completed carpentry apprenticeship with Certificate III as the entry requirement. For the existing workforce, provide a separate route through reliably verified equivalent competence and targeted training or experience for identified gaps. Tenure alone is not sufficient, and competent existing workers should not repeat a full qualification unnecessarily. This is our proposed entry rule, not a government decision. The historical RIS describes assessment and training plans for transition, but its settings require current confirmation. [2, pp. 71–72; 6, slide 6; 9]
after: For future entrants, this initiative recommends a completed carpentry apprenticeship with Certificate III as the normal baseline technical foundation. Recognise those assessed outcomes rather than routinely repeating a full trade test. If an additional licensing module or examination is proposed, specify the regulatory knowledge or competence gap it addresses and demonstrate its necessity. No compulsory additional exam or wholesale Certificate III redesign is selected here. Consider existing-building awareness in training only after mapping current coverage and any demonstrated gaps. [6, slide 4; 8]

before: • Assess competence against the required outcome, not merely possession of documents.
after: • Assess competence against the required outcome; qualifications and references are evidence, not substitutes for reliable verification where gaps remain.

For existing workers, missing apprenticeship records should not by itself exclude a competent applicant. Use verified work history, representative work evidence, corroborating references and practical assessment appropriate to the gaps. Require targeted training or experience where competence is not demonstrated; do not rely on tenure alone or make competent workers repeat a full qualification unnecessarily. The historical RIS describes transition assessment and training plans, but does not establish current adopted settings. [2, pp. 71–72; 9]

before: Set transition duration using cohort size, verified gaps, safety risk and regulator and training capacity. A five-year pathway was raised by a meeting participant and also appears in the historical RIS, with a time-limited application period and training-plan conditions. Neither source establishes a current adopted duration. Staging should not permit unproven safety-critical competence or become indefinite provisional status. [2, pp. 71–72; 5, DTPM-022 and 033; 7; 9]
after: Set transition duration using cohort size, verified gaps, safety risk and regulator and training capacity. A five-year pathway was raised by a meeting participant and appears in the historical RIS with an application window and training-plan conditions. Neither source establishes a current adopted duration. Avoid indefinite provisional status or unsupervised work where safety-critical competence remains unproven. [2, pp. 71–72; 5, DTPM-022 and 033; 7; 9]

Recognition of prior learning should retain the rigour needed to establish the required competence. Some providers advertise approximately three months for recognition of skills already acquired, not three months of novice trade training. Duration alone does not establish invalid assessment. Require authentic, current and sufficient evidence, reliable practical verification where needed, and targeted gap training. ASQA warns against inadequate assessment and misleading RPL marketing. Preserve legitimate recognition for experienced workers while addressing demonstrated assessment failures. [15–16]

before: Victoria should preserve a credible carpenter career pathway: apprenticeship and baseline trade competence, followed by advanced residential capability where a distinct need is demonstrated. Existing builder entry pathways remain directly available. Advanced recognition must never become a mandatory step before builder registration. Possible mechanisms include an endorsement, reform of Domestic Builder Limited to Carpentry, an optional Registered Residential Carpenter pathway, a non-statutory credential or no additional mechanism. Define the function, evidence and public benefit before choosing among them.
after: Victoria should preserve a credible carpenter career pathway: apprenticeship and baseline trade competence, appropriate additional requirements for independent business operation, and optional assessed progression for defined residential work where need and public benefit are demonstrated. Do not require the full builder pathway for every narrower function if a proportionate lawful alternative can meet the same consumer outcome. Existing builder entry pathways remain directly available; advanced recognition must never become mandatory before builder registration. An endorsement, reform of DB-L Carpentry, optional RRC, a non-statutory credential or no additional mechanism remain options. Additional statutory contracting authority would require an authorised mechanism, not merely a voluntary credential.

before: • For future entrants, completed carpentry apprenticeship and Certificate III evidence; for the existing workforce, verified equivalent competence and targeted gap training where needed.
after: • Completed apprenticeship and Certificate III outcomes normally establish future entrants’ baseline technical competence; justify additional checks by a specific regulatory purpose. For existing workers, verify equivalent competence with work evidence, references and practical assessment where needed, then address identified gaps.
